entry.title: [BIP Draft] Co-signer Spending Policies
entry.summary:
Co-signer spending policies for Bitcoin leverage the Taproot output structure, enabling multiple ways to authorize transactions. These mechanisms may require participant keys, signatures from a designated co-signer group, specific script-enforced conditions like timelocks, or a combination of these elements. The operational framework is defined by a single, portable policy document, uniquely identified, that delineates precisely which outputs co-signers can approve, the circumstances under which approval is allowed, and the nature of evidence required before any action is taken.
Bitcoin script is prioritized to handle all enforceable conditions autonomously, delegating only those tasks it cannot address—such as external price feeds or repayment confirmations—to human or automated co-signers. The co-signer group is constituted either as an all-must-sign MuSig2 aggregate key or as a k-of-n threshold scheme. In the latter case, an invalid transaction is prevented if a sufficient subset of co-signers (at least n−k+1) withhold their signatures.
Verification relies on attested evidence: trusted entities sign statements confirming facts like asset prices or loan repayments. Every co-signer must recognize existing Discreet Log Contract (DLC) oracle attestations, and there is an optional provision for these attestations to include a finality indicator. During the signing process in "open-v0" mode, the co-signer reviews the policy, the Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction (PSBT), and supporting evidence, verifying the policy ID, ensuring each output aligns with pre-approved templates, and checking that the evidence is timely, sufficiently attested, and finalized as required. The co-signer then proceeds to either sign or reject the transaction, providing all participants with a documented record of the decision.
A built-in escape mechanism ensures funds cannot become permanently inaccessible; there is always at least one method of spending coins without co-signer intervention, typically involving a lengthy timelock. For example, in a lending scenario, collateral may be released to the borrower upon confirmation of repayment, or liquidated if certain price or default triggers are met. Both borrower and lender retain the option to settle directly, while the borrower benefits from a long-timelock path for fund recovery.
This system does not involve any change to Bitcoin's consensus rules, nor does it yet support blinded verification or secure hardware enclaves, though such features are planned for future integration. Rather than rendering co-signers trustless, the framework aims to standardize their operating procedures, making them transparent and subject to public review.
